title: Only 1 in 4 Japanese Adults Trust Social Media
paragraphs: How much do you trust social media?

A survey done by The Yomiuri Shimbun and Waseda University has found that almost three out of four Japanese adults do not trust the information they see posted on social media platforms like YouTube and X. Or at least, they don't trust it very much.
The remaining one in four people do trust information shared on social media, though this includes those who say they only trust it a little.

Younger people are more likely to trust information shared on social media, with 38% of those aged 18 to 39 saying they do. This is compared with 28% of people aged 40 to 59, and just 14% of those aged 60 and above.
The survey also asked participants how they feel about several news topics, to see how much the public accepts certain unconventional views often shared on social media.
For example, 12% of participants agree with the belief that reducing greenhouse gas emissions is unnecessary. This grew to 22% among those who trust what's posted on social media.

This is despite strong consensus among scientists that global warming is the result of human activity and greenhouse gas emissions, and that urgent action is needed to keep the planet from becoming too hot.
Meanwhile, 27% of participants believe that offering economic assistance to developing countries does not serve Japan's national interests — while 69% think it does.

Belief in the purposefulness of this assistance rises to 74% among participants 60 and older. The Japanese government says such assistance contributes to its national interests by promoting global peace and stability.
And 11% say it's fine for the Japanese government to sell as many bonds as it wants to cover budget shortfalls — while economists believe there is a limit to how long this can work.
The percentage of survey participants who think it's OK to sell bonds indefinitely grew to 23% among those who trust social media.
